reference.source: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice / GeneReviews
clinicalPearls: Characterised by exercise-induced, painless muscle stiffness and impaired relaxation that worsens with continued activity and is often aggravated by cold
The delayed relaxation is a pseudomyotonia: it mimics myotonia clinically but is electrically silent on needle electromyography, unlike true myotonia
Stiffness typically affects the limbs, eyelids and face during and after exertion and eases with rest
Caused by mutations in ATP2A1 encoding the fast-twitch sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium ATPase SERCA1, most often inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern
Creatine kinase is usually normal or only mildly elevated and fixed weakness is not a prominent feature
There is a theoretical concern about calcium handling during anaesthesia, so the anaesthetic history and drug choice warrant attention
Because the electrical silence distinguishes it from true myotonias, correlating the clinical picture with electromyography is key to the diagnosis
reference.pathophysiology: Brody myopathy is caused by mutations in ATP2A1, which encodes SERCA1, the calcium ATPase of the sarcoplasmic reticulum in fast-twitch (type II) muscle fibres. SERCA1 pumps calcium from the cytoplasm back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum to terminate contraction and allow relaxation. When SERCA1 activity is deficient, cytoplasmic calcium is cleared too slowly after a contraction, so relaxation is delayed and repeated contractions cause cumulative stiffness, particularly during sustained or rapid exercise and in the cold. Because the impaired relaxation results from defective calcium reuptake rather than abnormal membrane excitability, the phenomenon is electrically silent, distinguishing it from the true myotonias.
additionalDifferentials: Metabolic myopathies causing exercise-induced cramps and contractures
additionalInvestigations: Needle electromyography demonstrating electrical silence during the clinically stiff, delayed relaxation (absence of myotonic discharges)
Serum creatine kinase, usually normal or mildly raised
Exercise and cooling provocation to reproduce the delayed relaxation
Muscle biopsy with assessment of SERCA1 expression and calcium ATPase activity
Assessment to exclude true myotonic disorders and metabolic myopathies
redFlags: Severe exertional stiffness limiting safe activity or, rarely, rhabdomyolysis with dark urine after intense exercise
Potential adverse calcium-handling responses during general anaesthesia
Bulbar or respiratory involvement, which would prompt reconsideration of the diagnosis
Progressive fixed weakness, which is atypical and suggests an alternative disorder
reference.prognosis: Brody myopathy is generally non-progressive and compatible with a normal lifespan, and although exercise-induced stiffness can be functionally limiting, most patients manage well with pacing of activity, warming-up and avoidance of cold.
pitfalls: Labelling the delayed relaxation as true myotonia without noting that electromyography is silent
Being reassured by a normal creatine kinase and dismissing a genuine muscle disorder
Overlooking the anaesthetic implications of abnormal calcium handling
Confusing it with metabolic myopathies that also cause exercise-induced contractures
references: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: Manage with activity modification: pacing exertion, thorough warm-up, and avoidance of cold exposure and sustained or rapid repetitive contraction
Consider a pharmacological trial of agents that ease muscle relaxation such as dantrolene or a calcium-channel blocker like verapamil
Provide physiotherapy with graded exercise to maintain function
Flag the anaesthetic risk from disordered calcium handling, avoiding triggering agents and planning malignant-hyperthermia-aware anaesthesia
Refer to a neuromuscular specialist and confirm the diagnosis with electrically silent electromyography and targeted ATP2A1 genetic testing
Offer genetic counselling and family screening given the autosomal recessive inheritance
